startup.name: RoboDock
startup.one_liner: Robots that run autonomous depots for autonomous fleets
startup.description: RoboDock builds robots that do depot work such as charging and vehicle checks for electric and autonomous vehicle fleets. Customers are fleet operators who pay to cut labor cost and raise vehicle uptime. Four person team in San Francisco.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate is about 1 percent (0.6 to 2 percent band, yc_acceptance.md). Test assumption: the company was accepted, so this note records the adjustments only. Up because robotaxi fleets are scaling and depot labor is a clear pain point. Down because the team is four people with no stated traction and hardware needs capital and pilots. Test note: accepted in fact, so this step is not scored.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because the pitch has no customer, pilot or demo behind it, and depot robotics for autonomous fleets depends on a few buyers such as robotaxi operators that may build in house. A hardware company also needs a long, expensive build before revenue.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --years 2022-2025 --industry Industrials: seed cond 67% (n=12, anecdote); upper bound seed about 64% for the broad cohort.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Industrials cohort has only 12 companies so I use the broad 57 percent cohort. Lowered slightly because a hardware team of four with no revenue needs proof from a pilot, and the round must exceed about $500K within 12 months.

bands.rationale: Small seed from robotics angels while building a first unit, near the lower seed raise quartile of $2.1M.
Typical 2022+ seed with a median raise near $3.3M and hardware premium for robotics.
Upside if a robotaxi operator signs a pilot, as robotics investors fund this theme.

ladder.why_it_fails: A round above $500K inside 12 months fails if there is no signed pilot with a fleet operator. Boost Robotics and Physical Turing, two comparable robotics YC companies, show seed money coming slowly or not at all, and investors dislike hardware with a few possible buyers.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --years 2022-2025 --industry Industrials: series_a cond 0% (n=8, anecdote) (broad 22%, n=115; B2B 26%, n=74).
anchors.adjustment_reason: At the broad cohort anchor of 22 percent. Held because Industrials in the data shows no Series A yet, though n is tiny.

bands.rationale: Thin A to pay for first deployments, near the 2018-2021 median of $10M.
Typical 2022+ A for robotics at about $15M raise.
Upside if it signs a large robotaxi depot contract.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A needs paying deployments with measurable uptime gains. The likely miss is a long pilot cycle with fleet operators and robots that cost more than the human labor they replace. AmpUp took five years from batch to a Series A even in EV charging, and Curo was absorbed by a strategic buyer without ever raising a large round.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --years 2022-2025 (broad cohort series_b cond 12%, n=25) and --years 2018-2021 --industry B2B (series_b cond 39%, n=18). Older cohort used because 2022+ is right censored.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the older B2B anchor because hardware and customer concentration slow growth, but above the thin recent rate.

bands.rationale: Thin B funding factory and fleet roll out, near $29M median.
Typical 2022+ B for robotics near $37M median.
Upside if it becomes the standard for robotaxi depots.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B needs repeatable installs in many depots. The risk is that large operators build depots in house or buy from a stronger funded rival, and that robot unit costs stay too high. Peers in charging, such as AmpUp, grew slowly and relied on strategic investors.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --years 2018-2021: series_c cond 30% (n=23), B2B 57% (n=7). Small n, wide range.
anchors.adjustment_reason: At the broad cohort anchor with a note that hardware lowers odds slightly.

bands.rationale: Thin growth round near the 2022+ median of $45M.
Typical growth round for a robotics infrastructure company.
Upside if autonomous fleets scale as hoped, sized against the stage benchmarks and cohort round medians for this round.

ladder.why_it_fails: Late rounds fail when autonomous fleets scale slower than forecast or when the largest operators bring depot work in house. A company selling to a handful of customers faces concentration risk, and few YC hardware companies with this buyer profile have reached Series C, so most outcomes end in a strategic sale instead.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the team never gets a paid fleet deployment because pilots are slow and robot cost beats labor only at large scale, or it is acquired for its team by a larger robotics or charging company. A billion dollar result needs autonomous fleets to scale and outsource depot work, which is uncertain.

killers.risk: Few buyers and they may build depot automation in house
killers.evidence: Robotaxi and large fleet operators control depots and have large engineering teams.
killers.mitigation: Sign a design partner early and keep the system modular.

killers.risk: Robots cost more than the labor they replace at pilot scale
killers.evidence: Depot work such as plugging and checks is done by low cost workers today, and robotics unit costs are high early.
killers.mitigation: Start with one task such as charging where uptime value is high.

killers.risk: Autonomous fleet rollout is slower than needed
killers.evidence: Demand depends on robotaxi growth which is regulated and uneven.
killers.mitigation: Serve electric delivery and transit fleets as well.

technical_complexity.rationale: Robots that plug in vehicles, inspect them and clear faults in messy real depots need perception, manipulation and safety work. A team of four can build a demo in months but a reliable product takes years and capital.

takeover_risk.rationale: Operators with large teams could build their own robots, and funded charging companies could add inspection. A rival needs about a year and a half to reach parity on reliability.

evidence.claim: Fleet operators and infrastructure builders are spending heavily on charging depots for electric and autonomous fleets

actions: Track uptime and labor hours saved
roadmap.proof: Documented labor cost saving above 30 percent

Hardware plus software is harder to copy than a software only idea

narrative.headline: A real but narrow depot robotics bet with few buyers and a long path to revenue.
narrative.general_summary: RoboDock wants to automate charging and checks at depots for electric and autonomous fleets. The need is real as robotaxi and electric fleets scale, but the team has four people, no stated traction and a hard hardware problem. Funding for robotics is available, yet a seed above $500K inside a year depends on a pilot with a named operator. Later steps are discounted because buyers are few, operators may build in house and unit economics against cheap depot labor are unproven. Data on industrials in recent cohorts is tiny, so uncertainty is wide.

assumptions: Only the batch listing was used, as of 2026-01-05.
Seed step means a round above about $500K within 12 months of the batch start.
Industrials cohort has 12 companies, so I used the broad cohort and note it is thin.
Market news dated after the as of date was ignored.
